resources.description:
World Resources Institute Aqueduct Floods baseline riverine model using historical data.

Riverine and coastal flood depth (in metres), unprotected -- i.e. with no allowance for flood defences -- at nine return periods: 1-in-2, 1-in-5, 1-in-10, 1-in-25, 1-in-50, 1-in-100, 1-in-250, 1-in-500 and 1-in-1000 years. Coverage is global, at a spatial resolution of 30 × 30 arc seconds (approx. 1 km at the equator). Riverine sets are available for a historical baseline (1980) and, for five GCMs, for RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 in 2030, 2050 and 2080; coastal sets are available with and without subsidence, at the 5th, 50th and 95th percentiles of sea level rise.

Produced by the [World Resources Institute (WRI) Aqueduct Floods](https://www.wri.org/aqueduct) project, building on the Global Flood Risk with IMAGE Scenarios (GLOFRIS) model. Source: Ward, P. J., et al. (2020). Aqueduct Floods Methodology. Technical Note. Washington, D.C.: World Resources Institute. <https://www.wri.org/research/aqueduct-floods-methodology>. Because flood defences are not represented, the indicator will tend to overstate depth and extent where defences exist.

resources.description:
Degree days indicators are calculated by integrating over time the amount by which the temperature
of the medium exceeds a reference temperature. The exact method of calculation may vary;
here the daily maximum near-surface temperature 'tasmax' is used to calculate an annual indicator:

$$
I^\text{dd} = \frac{365}{n_y} \sum_{d = 1}^{n_y} \max \left( T^\text{max}_d - T^\text{ref}, 0 \right), \qquad i^\text{dd} = \mathbb{E}(I^\text{dd}) \nonumber
$$

$i^\text{dd}$ is the indicator and $I^\text{dd}$ the degree days in a single year, $T^\text{max}_d$ is the daily maximum near-surface temperature for day index $d$, $n_y$ is the number of days in the year
and $T^\text{ref}$ is the reference temperature given in the indicator name (32°C by default).

The expectation is estimated by averaging over a 20-year window.

Downscaled climate simulations from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6), sourced from the [NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections](https://www.nccs.nasa.gov/services/data-collections/land-based-products/nex-gddp-cmip6).

Indicators are generated for periods: 'historical' (averaged over 1995-2015), 2030 (2020-2040), 2040 (2030-2050), and 2050 (2040-2060).

These data should not be used in any manner relating to emergency management or planning, public safety,
physical safety or property endangerment. For higher-resolution data based on up-to-date methods,
subject to greater validation, and suitable for bottom-up risk analysis please contact
[Jupiter Intelligence](https://www.jupiterintel.com).

This fire model computes the maximum monthly probability per annum of a wildfire within 100 km of
a given location based on several parameters from multiple bias corrected and downscaled Global Climate Models (GCMs).
For example, if the probability of occurrence of a wildfire is 5% in July, 20% in August, 10% in September
and 0% for other months, the hazard indicator value is 20%.

These data should not be used in any manner relating to emergency management or planning, public safety,
physical safety or property endangerment. For higher-resolution data based on up-to-date methods,
subject to greater validation, and suitable for bottom-up risk analysis please contact
[Jupiter Intelligence](https://www.jupiterintel.com).

This drought model is based on the Standardized Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI).
The SPEl is an extension of the Standardized Precipitation Index which also considers Potential Evapotranspiration (PET)
in determining drought events.
The SPEl is calculated from a log-logistic probability distribution function of climatic water balance
(precipitation minus evapotranspiration) over a given time scale.
The SPEI itself is a standardized variable with a mean value 0 and standard deviation 1.
This drought model computes the number of months per annum where the 3-month rolling average
of SPEI is below -2 based on the mean values of several parameters from
bias-corrected and downscaled multiple Global Climate Models (GCMs).

These data should not be used in any manner relating to emergency management or planning, public safety,
physical safety or property endangerment. For higher-resolution data based on up-to-date methods,
subject to greater validation, and suitable for bottom-up risk analysis please contact
[Jupiter Intelligence](https://www.jupiterintel.com).

This model computes the maximum daily water equivalent precipitation (in mm) measured at the 100 year
return period based on the mean of the precipitation distribution from multiple bias corrected and
downscaled Global Climate Models (GCMs).

These data should not be used in any manner relating to emergency management or planning, public safety,
physical safety or property endangerment. For higher-resolution data based on up-to-date methods,
subject to greater validation, and suitable for bottom-up risk analysis please contact
[Jupiter Intelligence](https://www.jupiterintel.com).

This hail model computes the number of days per annum where hail exceeding 5 cm diameter is possible
based on the mean distribution of several parameters
across multiple bias-corrected and downscaled Global Climate Models (GCMs).

These data should not be used in any manner relating to emergency management or planning, public safety,
physical safety or property endangerment. For higher-resolution data based on up-to-date methods,
subject to greater validation, and suitable for bottom-up risk analysis please contact
[Jupiter Intelligence](https://www.jupiterintel.com).

This heat model computes the number of days exceeding 35°C per annum based on the mean of distribution fits
to the bias-corrected and downscaled high temperature distribution
across multiple Global Climate Models (GCMs).

These data should not be used in any manner relating to emergency management or planning, public safety,
physical safety or property endangerment. For higher-resolution data based on up-to-date methods,
subject to greater validation, and suitable for bottom-up risk analysis please contact
[Jupiter Intelligence](https://www.jupiterintel.com).

This wind speed model computes the maximum 1-minute sustained wind speed (in m/s) experienced over a
100 year return period based on mean wind speed distributions
from multiple Global Climate Models (GCMs).

These data should not be used in any manner relating to emergency management or planning, public safety,
physical safety or property endangerment. For higher-resolution data based on up-to-date methods,
subject to greater validation, and suitable for bottom-up risk analysis please contact
[Jupiter Intelligence](https://www.jupiterintel.com).

Flooded fraction provides the spatial fraction of land flooded in a defined grid.
It is derived from higher-resolution flood hazards, and computed directly as the fraction of
cells within the 30-km cell that have non-zero flooding at that return period.
This model uses a 30-km grid that experiences flooding at the 200-year return period.
Open oceans are excluded.

The mean work loss indicator is calculated from the 'Wet Bulb Globe Temperature' (WBGT) indicator:

$$
I^\text{WBGT}_d = 0.567 \times T^\text{avg}_d + 0.393 \times p^\text{vapour}_d + 3.94
$$

$I^\text{WBGT}_d$ is the WBGT indicator, $T^\text{avg}_d$ is the average daily near-surface temperature (in degrees Celsius) on day index, $d$, and $p^\text{vapour}_d$
is the water vapour partial pressure (in kPa). $p^\text{vapour}$ is calculated from relative humidity $h^\text{relative}_d$ via:

$$
p^\text{vapour}_d = \frac{h^\text{relative}_d}{100} \times 6.105 \times \exp \left( \frac{17.27 \times T^\text{avg}_d}{237.7 + T^\text{avg}_d} \right)
$$

The work ability indicator, $I^{\text{WA}}_d$, is finally calculated via:

$$
I^{\text{WA}}_d = 0.1 + 0.9 / \left( 1 + (I^\text{WBGT}_d / \alpha_1)^{\alpha_2} \right)
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ depend on the work intensity: $(32.98, 17.81)$ for low, $(30.94, 16.64)$ for medium and $(24.64, 22.72)$ for high intensity.

The mean annual work loss indicator, $i^{\text{WL}}$, is calculated via:

$$
I^{\text{WL}} = 1 - \frac{1}{n_y} \sum_{d = 1}^{n_y} I^{\text{WA}}_d, \qquad i^{\text{WL}} = \mathbb{E}(I^{\text{WL}}),
$$

$I^{\text{WL}}$ being the work loss in a single year and $n_y$ the number of days in the year. The expectation is estimated by averaging over a 20-year window. The OS-Climate-generated indicators are inferred from CMIP6 data, averaged over 6 models: ACCESS-CM2, CMCC-ESM2, CNRM-CM6-1, MPI-ESM1-2-LR, MIROC6 and NorESM2-MM.
The indicators are generated for periods: 'historical' (averaged over 1995-2014), 2030 (2021-2040), 2040 (2031-2050) and 2050 (2041-2060).

Days per year for which the average near-surface temperature 'tas' is above a threshold specified in °C.

$$
I = \frac{365}{n_y} \sum_{d = 1}^{n_y} \boldsymbol{\mathbb{1}}_{\; \, T^\text{avg}_d > T^\text{ref}}, \qquad i = \mathbb{E}(I) \nonumber
$$

$i$ is the indicator and $I$ the number of days above the threshold in a single year, $T^\text{avg}_d$ is the daily average near-surface temperature for day index $d$ in °C, $n_y$ is the number of days in the year
and $T^\text{ref}$ is the reference temperature.

The expectation is estimated by averaging over a 20-year window.

Downscaled climate simulations from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6), sourced from the [NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections](https://www.nccs.nasa.gov/services/data-collections/land-based-products/nex-gddp-cmip6).

Indicators are generated for periods: 'historical' (averaged over 1995-2015), 2030 (2020-2040), 2040 (2030-2050), and 2050 (2040-2060).

Sparks, N., Toumi, R. The Imperial College Storm Model (IRIS) Dataset. *Sci Data* **11**, 424 (2024). <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-024-03250-y>

Assessing tropical cyclone risk on a global scale given the infrequency of landfalling tropical cyclones and the short period of reliable observations remains a challenge. Synthetic tropical cyclone datasets can help overcome these problems. Here we present a new global dataset created by IRIS, the ImpeRIal college Storm Model. IRIS is novel because, unlike other synthetic TC models, it only simulates the decay from the point of lifetime maximum intensity. This minimises the bias in the dataset. It takes input from 42 years of observed tropical cyclones and creates a 10,000 year synthetic dataset which is then validated against the observations. IRIS captures important statistical characteristics of the observed data. The return periods of the landfall maximum wind speed (1 minute sustained in m/s) are realistic globally. Climate model projections are used to adjust the life-time maximum intensity.

***Disclaimer***: There have been many improvements on the dataset. Contact Professor Toumi from the Imperial College London for improved data.

resources.display_name: Mean degree days above threshold in °C ({gcm})
resources.description:
Degree days indicators are calculated by integrating over time the amount by which the temperature
of the medium exceeds a reference temperature. The exact method of calculation may vary;
here the daily average near-surface temperature 'tas' is used to calculate an annual indicator for each of
a set of threshold (reference) temperatures, 16°C, 20°C and 24°C by default:

$$
I^\text{dd} = \frac{365}{n_y} \sum_{d = 1}^{n_y} \max \left( T^\text{avg}_d - T^\text{ref}, 0 \right), \qquad i^\text{dd} = \mathbb{E}(I^\text{dd}) \nonumber
$$

$i^\text{dd}$ is the indicator and $I^\text{dd}$ the degree days in a single year, $T^\text{avg}_d$ is the daily average near-surface temperature for day index $d$, $n_y$ is the number of days in the year
and $T^\text{ref}$ is the threshold temperature.

The expectation is estimated by averaging over a 20-year window.

resources.display_name: Weeks with average water temperature above threshold in °C ({gcm})
display_groups: Weeks with average water temperature above threshold in °C
resources.description:
Weeks per year for which the average water temperature is above a threshold specified in °C:

$$
I = \frac{52}{n_y} \sum_{w = 1}^{n_y} \boldsymbol{\mathbb{1}}_{\; \, T^\text{avg}_w > T^\text{ref}}, \qquad i = \mathbb{E}(I) \nonumber
$$

$i$ is the indicator and $I$ the number of weeks above the threshold in a single year, $T^\text{avg}_w$ is the weekly average water temperature for week index $w$ in °C, $n_y$ is the number of weeks in the year
and $T^\text{ref}$ is the reference temperature. The expectation is estimated by averaging over the years of each period listed below.

The OS-Climate-generated indicators are inferred from downscaled CMIP5 data. This is done for 5 Global Climate Models: GFDL-ESM2M, HadGEM2-ES, IPSL-CM5A-LR, MIROC-ESM-CHEM and NorESM1-M.
The downscaled data is sourced from the [Futurestreams dataset](https://geo.public.data.uu.nl/vault-futurestreams/research-futurestreams%5B1633685642%5D/original/waterTemp/) on the data publication platform of Utrecht University.
Indicators are generated for periods: 'historical' (averaged over 1976-2005), 2020 (2006-2030), 2030 (2021-2040), 2040 (2031-2050), 2050 (2041-2060), 2060 (2051-2070), 2070 (2061-2080), 2080 (2071-2090) and 2090 (2081-2100).

resources.display_name: Days with wet-bulb globe temperature above threshold in °C ({gcm})
display_groups: Days with wet-bulb globe temperature above threshold in °C
resources.description:
Days per year for which the 'Wet Bulb Globe Temperature' indicator is above a threshold specified in °C:

$$
I = \frac{365}{n_y} \sum_{d = 1}^{n_y} \boldsymbol{\mathbb{1}}_{\; \, T^\text{WBGT}_d > T^\text{ref}}, \qquad i = \mathbb{E}(I) \nonumber
$$

$i$ is the indicator and $I$ the number of days above the threshold in a single year, $d$ is the day index, $n_y$ is the number of days in the year and $T^\text{ref}$ is the reference temperature. The expectation is estimated by averaging over a 20-year window.

The 'Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature' (WBGT) indicator is calculated from both the average daily near-surface temperature in °C denoted $T^\text{avg}$ and the water vapour partial pressure in kPa denoted $p^\text{vapour}$:

$$
T^\text{WBGT}_d = 0.567 \times T^\text{avg}_d + 0.393 \times p^\text{vapour}_d + 3.94
$$

The water vapour partial pressure $p^\text{vapour}$ is calculated from relative humidity $h^\text{relative}$:

$$
p^\text{vapour}_d = \frac{h^\text{relative}_d}{100} \times 6.105 \times \exp \left( \frac{17.27 \times T^\text{avg}_d}{237.7 + T^\text{avg}_d} \right)
$$

The OS-Climate-generated indicators are inferred from downscaled CMIP6 data, averaged over 6 Global Climate Models: ACCESS-CM2, CMCC-ESM2, CNRM-CM6-1, MPI-ESM1-2-LR, MIROC6 and NorESM2-MM.
The downscaled data is sourced from the [NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections](https://www.nccs.nasa.gov/services/data-collections/land-based-products/nex-gddp-cmip6).
Indicators are generated for periods: 'historical' (averaged over 1995-2014), 2030 (2021-2040), 2040 (2031-2050), 2050 (2041-2060), 2060 (2051-2070), 2070 (2061-2080), 2080 (2071-2090) and 2090 (2081-2100).

The World Resources Institute (WRI) [Aqueduct 4.0](https://www.wri.org/data/aqueduct-global-maps-40-data) is the latest iteration of [WRI’s water risk framework](https://www.wri.org/data/aqueduct-water-risk-atlas) designed to translate complex
hydrological data into intuitive indicators of water-related risk:

- **Water demand**: gross demand is the maximum potential water required to meet sectoral demands. Sectoral water demand includes: domestic, industrial, irrigation, and livestock. Demand is displayed as a flux (centimetres/year).

- **Water supply**: available blue water, the total amount of renewable freshwater available to a sub-basin with upstream consumption removed, includes surface flow, interflow, and groundwater recharge. Available blue water is displayed as a flux (centimetres/year).

- **Water stress**: an indicator of competition for water resources defined informally as the ratio of demand for water by human society divided by available water. It can be classified into six categories: -1: Arid and low water use, 0: Low (<10%), 1: Low-medium (10-20%), 2: Medium-high (20-40%), 3: High (40-80%), 4: Extremely high (>80%).

- **Water depletion**: the ratio of total water consumption to available renewable water supplies. Total water consumption includes domestic, industrial, irrigation, and livestock consumptive uses. Available renewable water supplies include the impact of upstream consumptive water users and large dams on downstream water availability. Higher values indicate larger impact on the local water supply and decreased water availability for downstream users. Water depletion is similar to water stress; however, instead of looking at total water demand, water depletion is calculated using consumptive withdrawal only. It can be classified into six categories: -1: Arid and low water use, 0 : Low (<5%), 1: Low-medium (5-25%), 2 : Medium-high (25-50%), 3: High (50-75%), 4 : Extremely high (>75%).

[Aqueduct 4.0 FAQ](https://github.com/wri/Aqueduct40/blob/master/data_FAQ.md) explains why the water supply and demand values are measured as fluxes instead of volumes. Volumes (cubic metres) can vary significantly based on the size of each sub-basin, potentially misleading as they might primarily reflect a larger geographical area rather than indicating a higher rate of water flow. On the other hand, fluxes (centimetres/year), which measure the rate of water flow, offer a more direct and equitable means of comparing water availability between different sub-basins. Volume = Flux × Area.

The spatial resolution is 5 × 5 arc minutes which equates roughly to 10 kilometre (km) × 10 km pixels.
The future projections were created using CMIP6 climate forcings based on three future scenarios: optimistic (ssp126), business-as-usual (ssp370), and pessimistic (ssp585) available at [HYPFLOWSCI6](https://public.yoda.uu.nl/geo/UU01/YM7A5H.html). WRI's original data are presented at the HydroBASINS Level 6 scale. Indicators are available for periods: 'historical' (averaged over 1979-2019), 2030 (2015-2045), 2050 (2035-2065) and 2080 (2065-2095).

Note on historical water demand and water supply: Aqueduct 4.0 publishes water demand and water supply for the future projections only; its baseline (1979-2019) data include the water stress and water depletion ratios but not demand or supply themselves. The 'historical' water demand and water supply values are therefore derived rather than Aqueduct 4.0 baseline data: they are the Aqueduct 4.0 optimistic (ssp126) 2030 projection divided by the 2030 change-from-baseline ratio (business-as-usual, SSP2 RCP4.5) of the earlier [Aqueduct Water Stress Projections](https://www.wri.org/data/aqueduct-water-stress-projections-data) (2015). They should be treated as approximate, and are not fully consistent with the historical water stress and water depletion values.

resources.description:
Expected months per year for which the 12 month Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) is below a threshold.

$$
I = \sum_{m = 1}^{12} \mathbb{1}_{\; \, S_m < s^\text{thresh}}, \qquad i = \mathbb{E}(I) \nonumber
$$

$i$ is the indicator and $I$ the number of months below the threshold in a single year, $S_m$ is the 12 month SPEI for the month with index $m$ and $s^\text{thresh}$ is the threshold index.

The expectation is estimated by averaging over a 20-year window.

Unprotected flood depth for riverine floods occurring in Europe in the present and future climate.
Based on the CLMcom-CCLM4-8-17-EC-EARTH regional climate simulation (EURO-CORDEX), sets are available for RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5
for projected (central) years 2035 and 2085. The set has a spatial resolution of 100 m and comprises return periods of
10, 30, 100, 300 and 1000 years.

The [river flood data set](https://data.4tu.nl/datasets/df7b63b0-1114-4515-a562-117ca165dc5b) is part of the
[RAIN data set](https://data.4tu.nl/collections/1e84bf47-5838-40cb-b381-64d3497b3b36)
(Risk Analysis of Infrastructure Networks in Response to Extreme Weather); see also the
[RAIN project report D2.5](http://rain-project.eu/wp-content/uploads/2016/09/D2.5_REPORT_final.pdf).

Unprotected flood depths are combined from the 'River_flood_depth_X_Y_Z_R' data sets.
Standard of protection data is separately available using the 'River_flood_extent_X_Y_Z_with_protection' data set
(which makes use of the FLOPROS database), which provides protected flood extent.

resources.description: Global data set of protection levels for riverine and coastal flood, based on the [FLOPROS database](https://nhess.copernicus.org/articles/16/1049/2016/). For each of coastal and riverine inundation, the dataset provides for every location a minimum ("min") and maximum ("max") protection, specified as a return period in years; the min and max reflect uncertainty in the protection level. The return period indicates that the location is protected against flood events with that return period (e.g. 100 years indicates that the location is protected against 1-in-100 year flood events).

Land subsidence rate (millimetres/year), a global map for the historical period at a spatial resolution of 30 × 30 arc seconds (approx. 1 km at the equator), estimated with a deep learning model trained on observed subsidence and environmental covariates (see [paper](https://doi.org/10.1029/2023GL104497)).

Land subsidence -- gradual settlement or rapid sinking of the ground -- can occur as a result of natural factors (e.g., volcanic or seismic activity, collapse of subsurface cavities, compaction of loose fine-grained deposits) or anthropogenic activities (e.g., excessive groundwater abstraction, mining, subsurface energy extraction).

resources.description:
Maximum 10 metre 3 second gust peak wind speed (note 3 second average; by default physrisk wind speeds are 1 minute average) for different return periods, inferred from the Copernicus WISC European storm event set.

<https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/datasets/sis-european-wind-storm-synthetic-events?tab=overview>

The WISC dataset contains a set of synthetic windstorm events consisting of 22,980 individual
storm footprints over Europe. These are a physically realistic set of plausible windstorm
events based on the modelled climatic conditions, calculated using the Met Office HadGEM3 model
(Global Atmosphere 3 and Global Land 3 configurations).
Return period maps of peak gust wind speed are inferred from this data.

resources.description:
This spatial dataset provides annual probabilities of fire occurrence across Europe under both historical
conditions (2002–2022) and projected future climates (2023–2050) for two emissions pathways (RCP 4.5 and
RCP 8.5). It builds upon the methodology presented in **“Climate Change Risk Indicators for Central Banking:
Explainable AI in Fire Risk Estimations”** (https://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.4865384) and integrates a range of
high-quality geospatial layers to deliver wall-to-wall coverage at ~2.5 km resolution.

Annual probabilities were estimated by training XGBoost models with monotonic constraints on FWI-related features,
using historical fire occurrence as the target, followed by probability calibration and spatial application
to each year's input layers.

**Key input layers**

* **Fire Weather Index (FWI) v1.0** — [Copernicus Climate Data Store](
https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/datasets/sis-tourism-fire-danger-indicators?tab=overview)
* **Burned-area product (MCD64A1 v6.1)** — [NASA/USGS LP DAAC](https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/products/mcd64a1v061/)
* **Land-cover product (MCD12Q1 v6)** — [NASA/USGS LP DAAC](https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/products/mcd12q1v006/)
* **Critical infrastructure (HARCI-EU)** — Koks et al. (2019), *Scientific Data*
<https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-019-0135-1>
* **Urban centres & population** — [Geoapify](https://www.geoapify.com/)

For implementing the processing pipeline, we also leveraged the [CLAIMED library](https://github.com/claimed-framework/component-library), developed by IBM. CLAIMED provides a fully modular,
scalable architecture in which each stage of the workflow is encapsulated as a decoupled component; this greatly simplifies maintenance,
parallel execution, and automatic versioning. By using CLAIMED, we can natively integrate distributed-processing engines (e.g. Dask)
and orchestrators like Airflow, ensuring full transparency, reproducibility, and rapid adaptability whenever data sources
or model requirements evolve.

**Countries covered (ISO alpha-2 codes)**
AL, AT, BE, BG, CH, CY, CZ, DE, DK, EE, ES, FI, FR, GB, GR, HR, HU, IE, IS, IT, LI, LT, LU, LV, ME, MK, MT, NL, NO, PL, PT, RO, RS, SE, SI, SK, TR

River flood depth (in metres), unprotected -- i.e. with no allowance for flood defences -- at six return periods: 1-in-10, 1-in-20, 1-in-50, 1-in-100, 1-in-200 and 1-in-500 years. Coverage spans most of continental Europe together with the river basins draining into the Mediterranean and Black Seas across the Caucasus, Middle East and Northern Africa, at 100 m resolution.

Produced by the European Commission's [Joint Research Centre (JRC)](https://data.jrc.ec.europa.eu/dataset/1d128b6c-a4ee-4858-9e34-6210707f3c81). Source: Dottori, F., Alfieri, L., Bianchi, A., Skoien, J., and Salamon, P. (2022). A new dataset of river flood hazard maps for Europe and the Mediterranean Basin. *Earth System Science Data*, 14, 1549–1569. <https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-14-1549-2022>. Depths are simulated river discharges (LISFLOOD) routed onto the terrain with a hydrodynamic model (LISFLOOD-FP), without representing flood defences, so the indicator will tend to overstate depth and extent where defences exist. Dottori et al. (2022) compare the resulting maps against official, defended flood hazard maps for Hungary, Italy (Po basin), Norway, Spain and England: at the 1-in-100-year return period they capture, on average, around two-thirds of the reference flood extent, with the largest overstatement at return periods below 100 years.
